summary: This document is a best current practice describing how to get the most from the Internet White Pages Service using the protocols, products and procedures of its day. It invites discussion and suggestions for improvement.

plainLanguage.summary: Advice on how to run a good phone book that people can look up online.

questions: how to deploy white pages directory
what is the internet white pages service
why use x.500 for white pages
subtitle: A 1997 best-practice guide to publishing people's public contact details in an online directory, mainly with X.500 and LDAP.

tldr.problem: Internet users need to find each other's addresses, but self-registered or centralized white pages services collect haphazard data that ages quickly and is not kept up to date.
tldr.mechanism: Each organization publishes public address information about its own people in a local database, joined to others through a directory protocol. X.500 is the recommended protocol, with LDAP access, and lookups should be free.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Best Current Practice of its day and says it will be updated as new technology is proven. It is not marked as obsoleted in the unit metadata.

today: RFC 2148 is a Best Current Practice published in September 1997, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its figures and product advice reflect 1996 and 1997, and it says it would be revised as new technology matured.

sections.title: What the White Pages Service Is
sections.content:
A White Pages Service is a directory service offering Internet address information about people and organizations. The RFC calls the Internet version the IWPS and says the Internet is only effective if users can find each other's addresses.

The authors note that services built on self-registration of users or on centralized servers tend to gather data in a haphazard fashion, and that the data ages rapidly. The most vital attempts instead use distributed local databases, each holding a manageable part of the information, with a directory protocol on top that connects them and gives users access.

At the time of writing, X.500 was the most popular protocol, connecting the address information of about 1,5 million individuals and 3,000 organizations. Whois++ was second. The RFC also mentions Ph, with over 300 registered databases, but does not consider it a good candidate because it is not interconnected.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one giant phone book that nobody keeps tidy, many small phone books are kept by the people who know the entries best, and they are linked together so you can search them all.

sections.title: The Recommendations
sections.content:
The summary section lists five recommendations for organizations, using the RFC 2119 key words. An organization SHOULD publish public E-mail addresses and other public address information about its users, and should follow the privacy recommendations of a cited report on directory services and privacy. The preferred data structure and naming scheme is X.500, and the organization MAY also publish through others such as Whois++.

The organization SHOULD make the data available to LDAP clients by letting LDAP servers access it, and SHOULD NOT attempt to charge for simple access.

Other parties get advice too. E-mail vendors SHOULD build in LDAP lookup. Internet service providers SHOULD help smaller organizations, for example by hosting their data. All interested parties SHOULD make sure a core X.500 name space exists and that all names in it are resolvable.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are: share the public contact details you have, be careful with privacy, use the standard directory system, let others search it, and do not charge for looking things up.

sections.title: Who Publishes What
sections.content:
Information about a person should be published and maintained by an organization with a direct, durable link to that person: their employer, their school, or the service provider they subscribe to. Collecting and updating the data should always stay in the hands of the organization the information relates to, even if an Internet service provider hosts the database for it.

At a minimum the entry for an individual should hold the name, the e-mail address in RFC-822 format (or other contact information if there is none) and some indication of the person's relationship with the maintainer. Phone number, fax number, postal address and home page URL may be added. For organizations, the RFC lists the home page URL, postal address, fax numbers, Internet domain and the various names and abbreviations people may search for.

One drawback is noted: because X.500 entries for individuals sit under an organization, people can only be found if the searcher knows the organization, such as the service provider. A future index service is expected to ease this.
sections.plainLanguage: The school or company that knows you best writes your entry, keeps it fresh and shares only what is needed, like your name and how to reach you.

sections.title: Data Management, Legal Issues and Free Lookups
sections.content:
Keeping data up to date is a task that must not be underestimated for larger organizations. The RFC advises getting executive-level commitment, deciding what information to hold and its quality criteria (timeliness, update frequency, correctness), and reusing existing internal databases. An organization must filter out local information that is not meant for the public service.

Privacy laws vary by country, and a maintainer should follow the national law where the database resides. Even without legal pressure, the RFC asks maintainers to publish only correct information, let people view their own entries and withhold or change information, and not publish data just because it is there.

The RFC strongly recommends that all user lookups be free. Its reasons: micropayment technology is not available, subscription services have unacceptably high overhead, and current directory protocols do not support authentication at a level suitable for a charging service. This does not stop the same dataset supporting other services that charge.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the phone book correct, follow the privacy rules, and let people check or fix their own entry. Looking someone up should cost nothing.

sections.title: Why X.500, the Global Name Space and LDAP
sections.content:
The RFC recommends X.500 as the directory protocol, based on the 1988 standard plus Internet-specific additions. Its service, coordinated by Dante and called NameFLOW-Paradise, was the widest deployment. X.500 requires unique names, which is most easily met by a single-rooted naming tree, the Directory Information Tree.

The RFC says to use the global name space rather than a private X.500 namespace, warning that data may need significant restructuring later, much as with private IP addresses. It also says the name space is only manageable with a single root context under a cooperative agreement, and that turf battles over its control would ruin service quality.

It also recommends LDAP, the access protocol that offers the most X.500 functionality where implementing the full OSI stack is not feasible. A concerted effort to make LDAP available is the publication method that gives the widest access. Replication between databases is encouraged for performance, but restricted to country and organization entries and knowledge references because of privacy law.

X.500 is not recommended for a large-scope Yellow Pages service, for searching for a person without knowing the organization, or for character sets beyond ASCII, some Latin-based European scripts and Japanese.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors pick one shared directory system, with one shared top of the tree so names never clash, and a simpler way (LDAP) for ordinary programs to ask it questions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists several risks of having a directory. People may collect information for unintended purposes such as publishing directories, headhunting or harassing phone calls. They may try to reach more than you meant to publish, or change your data, sometimes by mistake rather than malice.

It gives three defenses. First, publish only what you can live with being public. Second, impose access control; LDAP supports a few methods including cleartext passwords, which are not secure against eavesdroppers, so stronger mechanisms are encouraged if modification is allowed over the open Internet, and otherwise modification should stay on the local intranet. Third, limit returned search items or refuse list operations where they are not useful, though such limits are rarely completely successful.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything in a public phone book can be misused, so only list what you are happy for everyone to see, and lock down who can change entries.

sections.title: Future Developments Foreseen in 1996
sections.content:
The RFC looks ahead from October 1996. It names a Common Indexing Protocol that would integrate X.500, Whois++ and stand-alone databases and enable yellow pages style searches. It also mentions stand-alone LDAP servers, an LDAP-to-DAP gateway, and a common core schema for multiple White Pages services.

The 1993 X.500 standard had been implemented in several products but not in NameFLOW-Paradise, mainly because it does not recognize a single root DSA. An enhancement to make a single root possible was proposed, with experiments expected in 1997. The RFC says later versions of the BCP may reference these developments once they stabilize.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors expected better ways to search all the phone books at once, and promised to update the advice when the new tools were ready.
